beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: What if abundance makes a civilization's appetite faster, without making it satisfied?

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Wendigo asks why greater capability does not automatically teach us when to stop.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: This is a philosophical systems argument, not a supernatural horror story.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: It connects cultural images of hunger with competition, institutions and technological power.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The practical question is how a society can preserve the conditions it depends on.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: You are invited to examine the difference between meeting needs and extending appetite.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: That distinction gives the book its purpose, and its uncomfortable force.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The book begins by placing a limit on its own use of mythology.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Its title draws from living Indigenous traditions that are neither interchangeable nor decorative.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The introduction explains why a generic antlered forest monster would miss the point.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The relevant connection concerns hunger, reciprocity and obligations that support communal survival.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The author develops a narrower systems hypothesis from that encounter.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The traditions do not become scientific evidence merely because their images are powerful.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Reading begins with that distinction, which governs the rest of the argument.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Imagine a community whose food must last through a difficult winter.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: One person's excess can reduce the margin protecting someone else's next meal.
